source.title: Is Feature Diversity Necessary in Neural Network Initialization?
source.authors: Yaniv Blumenfeld; Dar Gilboa; Daniel Soudry

record.file_problem: Full text provided; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains networks with reduced or identical initialization diversity and measures training/test outcomes, testing initialization effects relevant to V4 and training success under special initialization relevant to V3. Its initialization and architectures differ from the versions’ specified comparisons.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own MNIST replicated-feature experiment and CIFAR Constnet training results. Cited findings about Delta Orthogonal, Fixup, and other prior work are not rows. Figure 1 reports test error, not training classification error; the CIFAR results report test accuracy, not training error.
record.test_reason: The study uses He initialization, residual connections and Fixup-inspired design to investigate initial feature diversity. Its results concern test performance and symmetry breaking, rather than the training error, depth degradation, initialization-dependent speed or trainable depth specified by V1–V6. Its own initialization experiments therefore do not test these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that initial feature diversity may be unnecessary given an appropriate architecture and symmetry breaking: Constnet can match standard-initialization test performance. In the shallow MNIST experiment, reduced diversity harms test performance, and a small independent noise component removes that effect.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses replicated-feature initialization in a shallow MNIST network and a custom symmetric, mostly zero-initialized residual CNN on CIFAR; it does not use the specific original recipes and training-error measures in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: MNIST results depend on initial feature count, width, and added noise (lambda=0.01); Constnet symmetry breaking depends on stochastic computation or dropout, and batch normalization is retained for robustness to hyperparameter changes.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial feature count strongly predicts fixed-step MNIST test error; increasing width with fixed feature count gives saturating benefits and can eventually worsen performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial feature diversity affects final test performance in the tested shallow MNIST network.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an independent initialization component with lambda=0.01 removes the replicated-feature test-error effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small initialization noise can remove the test-performance penalty from replicated initial features in this MNIST setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Constnet with identical initial features and mostly zero weights achieves test performance described as matching standard initialization when symmetry can break.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial feature diversity is unnecessary for strong test performance in the tested residual architecture with a symmetry-breaking mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: With no dropout and deterministic computation preserving the initial symmetry, Constnet does not train.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested fully symmetric Constnet initialization requires a mechanism that breaks symmetry during training.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports test accuracies from 10.0% to 95.5% across initialization and dropout configurations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test performance of the tested ResNet-like architecture depends on the combination of initialization symmetry and symmetry-breaking conditions.

record.problems: The study primarily reports test accuracy/error rather than training classification error. Figure 1 lacks numeric values in the text. The CIFAR-100 numerical result is figure-only, and Appendix Table 1 is flattened so initialization settings cannot be assigned reliably. The special initialization requires stochastic symmetry breaking; deterministic symmetry-preserving training does not occur.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error under random initialization, including corrupted labels, and its dependence on size, stopping or regularization.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and their reduction with extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with plain-network depth, prevention by identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh training, and training residual networks without normalization.
Activation-matched signal and gradient propagation, learning-speed and trainable-depth comparisons, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and 10,000-layer plain convolutional training.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss growth, curvature adaptation, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
Controlled normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, including Fixup training without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3/V4 limits_scope labels confuse untested components with demonstrated limitations and should be removed. Original-source findings discussed in the introduction are cited background. Table 1's configuration marks require interpretation, but its supplied text preserves more row structure than the record acknowledges; the unrecorded 0.1-dropout, 95.2% result bears on no listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training error, model size, and early stopping are not measured.
No two-layer teacher-student ReLU problem or spurious-minimum frequency is tested.
The study does not compare plain networks with identity shortcuts for depth-related training error. CIFAR Constnet retains residual connections; its results do not measure training error.
The paper tests replicated/identical features and added noise, not activation-matched initialization, signal/gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, or trainable depth.
No learning-rate stability threshold, curvature, or catapult/edge-of-stability dynamics are tested.
Batch normalization is present in Constnet but is not compared against an otherwise identical network without it; speed and learning-rate tolerance are not tested.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.size_stated: hidden width N varied; K=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048 initial features
rows.operation_detail: Train with replicated He-initialized features; measure test error after 7500 SGD steps
rows.baseline: Standard initialization comparison not stated as a numerical baseline
rows.value: Figure 1: figure only; text says number of features upon initialization was the strongest indicator of success and increasing width without new features helped smaller networks but saturated, with wider networks sometimes performing worse.
rows.uncertainty: Error bars detailed in Figure 3; numeric uncertainty not stated in text.
rows.note: Figure 1 shows test error rather than training error. The text describes width effects and states that feature count was the strongest indicator, but no precise plotted values are transcribed.
rows.check: Fixed-step test error measures the effect of initial feature diversity on generalization; it does not establish V4's learning-speed or trainable-depth effect.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.size_stated: hidden width N varied; K=2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048 initial features
rows.operation_detail: Train with replicated He-initialized features plus a small i.i.d. component; measure test error after 7500 SGD steps
rows.value: Figure 1: figure only; text says the effect of replicated features vanishes completely at lambda=0.01.
rows.note: The reported effect is on test error; text explicitly says the replicated-feature effect vanishes with this noise level.
rows.check: The disappearance of the replicated-feature test-error penalty with added noise does not measure V4's signal-propagation, training-speed or depth claims.

rows.subject: Constnet
rows.size_stated: 12 residual layers; network widened ×10 after every 4 layers
rows.operation_detail: Train with symmetry-preserving initialization and no dropout, in deterministic mode to eliminate floating-point symmetry breaking
rows.baseline: Stochastic standard GPU computation and floating-point errors break symmetry; exact baseline outcome not quantified
rows.value: Training did not occur at all when symmetry could not be broken
rows.note: This control isolates the need for a symmetry-breaking mechanism in the special initialization; no training error measurement is supplied.
rows.check: Failure to train under exact symmetry establishes a need for symmetry breaking in Constnet, not any specified version. It is a clear failure for that separate question, rather than a partial V3/V4 effect.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The special residual architecture attained test accuracy matching the standard-initialized counterpart, but training error and plain-network depth degradation were not measured (R3-R5). Exact CIFAR-100 comparison is unclear (R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MNIST replicated-feature network and CIFAR Constnet
reader_labels.reason: The MNIST experiment found replicated-feature effects on test error that vanished with lambda=0.01, while Constnet attained matching test accuracy under highly symmetric initialization; the results do not test activation-matched or orthogonal initialization claims about speed/depth (R1-R5).
